sentences.t: The Reserve Bank of India describes the hundi as a credit instrument that evolved in India, most widely used in the 12th century and still around in modern times.
The Economic Times, quoting that description, lists three jobs a hundi did: send funds from one place to another, work as a loan, and finance trade as a bill of exchange.
The forms were specific.
A darshani hundi was payable the moment it was shown.
A muddati hundi was payable after a stated period or on a fixed date.
A jokhami hundi tied payment to the safe arrival of goods, which makes it close to a primitive insurance contract.
A trader choosing between them was choosing between speed, delay and risk.
The paper was never the point.
The point was the network of merchants and bankers who knew each other's credit well enough to honour it.
That is the part worth keeping.
The ET piece is careful to say a hundi was not simply an old-fashioned piece of paper.
It worked because the instrument was backed by merchants and indigenous bankers who understood one another's reputation.
It cites the historian Claude Markovits, whose work on trading communities such as the Shikarpuris shows how such networks moved capital across borders and kept relationships alive far from home.
The ET writer also says the hundi was not an early version of UPI.
I agree with that.
But it faced a problem that survives every technology since: how do you move value without moving the money?
Alongside these indigenous networks the British built a formal one.
The Bank of Bengal was set up in 1806, the Bank of Bombay in 1840 and the Bank of Madras in 1843.
In 1921 the three Presidency Banks merged into the Imperial Bank of India.
The Reserve Bank of India began operating on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act of 1934, and was nationalised on 1 January 1949.
ET sums up the situation in 1947 neatly: India had two financial histories running at once, one of trust networks and one of formal banking.
After Independence the question changed.
It was no longer only how money moved, but who could get into the system that moved it.
The Imperial Bank became the State Bank of India in 1955.
On 19 July 1969 the government nationalised 14 major banks, and six more in 1980.
RBI data quoted by ET show branches growing from 8,262 in 1969 to 59,752 by March 1990.
Lead bank schemes, regional rural banks and priority-sector lending pushed formal finance toward people it had never reached.
Still, the branch stayed at the centre.
To move money you often had to go to a counter, fill a form, hand over a cheque and wait while paper travelled between institutions.
The hundi had been replaced by a better-governed, wider piece of paper, but the shape was the same.
Electronic payment came in stages, and each stage is easy to miss because payment infrastructure is mostly invisible.
RTGS went live on 26 March 2004, first for transfers between banks.
NEFT followed in November 2005 and gave ordinary customers a nationwide electronic transfer.
The Payment and Settlement Systems Act of 2007 gave the whole area a legal framework.
NPCI was incorporated in 2008 as an umbrella body for retail payments.
Immediate Payment Service, IMPS, arrived in 2010 with round-the-clock interbank transfers.
There was a catch.
Faster rails are useless to people with nothing to pay from.
The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana was announced on 15 August 2014 and launched on 28 August.
By 22 July 2026, official data quoted by ET show 58.84 crore beneficiaries, ₹3.11 lakh crore in their accounts and 41.01 crore RuPay debit cards issued.
Add Aadhaar for identity and the mobile phone as the access point, and you get the layers the SBI executive Rama Mohan Rao Amara calls the JAM trinity, Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and Mobile.
UPI is built on top of them.
UPI went live as a pilot on 11 April 2016, with then RBI Governor Raghuram Rajan launching it in Mumbai.
Twenty-one banks took part.
The idea was a common platform for instant push and pull payments, linking several bank accounts through one interface.
It reused what existed: IMPS for instant transfer, banks for the accounts, the phone for the screen.
What it added was interoperability.
The scale since is hard to take in.

The PIB release says annual transactions went from about 2 crore in 2016-17 to 24,162 crore in 2025-26, a rise of nearly 12,000 times, while annual value went from ₹0.07 lakh crore to about ₹314 lakh crore.
The Economic Times, citing NPCI, puts July 2026 at 23.66 billion transactions worth ₹29.88 lakh crore.
The World Bank gives the comparison.
Between July and September 2025, it says, UPI processed about 59 billion transactions, more than Mastercard's global total of roughly 54 billion and approaching Visa's roughly 82 billion.
In 2024 UPI alone handled 172.2 billion transactions, against a combined 79.8 billion across the fast payment systems of eleven Latin American and Caribbean countries, Brazil's Pix included.
Now look at the sign above.
It is a banner on a post in a park.
It has no counter, no staff and no opening hours.
The SBI executive's column calls the QR code at a roadside tea stall "perhaps the smallest branch of India's financial system".
The government figure behind that: 86% of person-to-merchant transactions in 2025-26 were below ₹500.
The tiny payment is the product.
Large transfers were already possible through banks.
It is tempting to say UPI is faster.
It is, but the hundi was also faster than carrying coins, and the NEFT transfer was faster than a cheque.
Speed does not explain a country switching habits.
The World Bank authors give a better account.
Their point is that India turned instant payments from a tool for large bank-to-bank settlement into a service for everyone.
Earlier mobile money systems showed that simple phone payments could spread, but most were run by one provider and did not work with each other.
India's move was to make the system open and interoperable, and to let non-bank apps compete on how it felt to use.
They write that the real revolution was not technology alone but how technology is felt by people.
The SBI column puts the same thing in one line: "UPI did not simply digitise cash.
It digitised trust." A hundi trusted a network of merchants.
A branch trusted a building and a passbook.
UPI asks you to trust a mobile number, a virtual payment address or a square code, enough to settle a promise between two people who may never meet.
The column, I should say, is written by an executive of the country's largest bank, so read the praise with that in mind.
But the same line about trust is what the hundi era ran on.
Each generation found a new way to let strangers trust a promise.
The paper, the building, the rail and the code are the packaging.
Both the World Bank and the SBI column end on cautions, not victory laps.
The World Bank names operational resilience, concentration risk that could hurt competition, transparency for users and open finance.
The SBI column adds fraud: social engineering, mule accounts, synthetic identities and AI-enabled scams.
It also raises a question about data.
A richer digital footprint should widen a citizen's choices, it argues, not narrow them, which is why consent and purpose limits matter.
Two numbers show how fast the system is still changing.
The column says more than 800 million UPI transactions worth over ₹35,000 crore in July 2026 were authenticated by fingerprint or face.
It also says UPI now runs in nine countries, with Cambodia the latest in 2026.
The PIB release lists eight countries, and gives 703 banks live on UPI as of March 2026 against the column's 741 in August.
The gap is probably timing, but I cannot confirm that from either source.
Where the sources differPIB (30 April 2026): 703 banks live, 8 countries accepting UPI.
SBI column (24 August 2026): 741 banks, 9 countries.
The PIB release also has internal inconsistencies in its launch-month figures, so I used only its annual numbers.
A hundi worked because the merchants behind it were known.
The next problem is making that true for a small shopkeeper whose digital receipts have never counted as proof of anything.
The SBI column imagines using consented payment data, GST information and RBI's Unified Lending Interface to help lenders judge such borrowers better.
It is a hope, not a result, and it is written by one bank's executive.
This section is my reading, not something the sources say.
Three things from the history look relevant to your work.
First, the jokhami hundi.
India had a payment instrument that bundled a transfer with a risk condition, payable on safe arrival of goods.
Payments and risk cover were close relatives long before the two industries separated.
Second, the pattern that worked.
UPI built open rails, let banks and non-banks plug in, and competed on the experience above them.
That is the argument the World Bank makes, and it is the same argument the insurance distribution fight turns on: who is allowed to build on top, and what the economics look like when they do.
It is a useful lens for the IRDAI commission-cap debate in today's paper.
Third, the limit.
The rails made payments effortless.
They did not by themselves make credit or cover effortless.
If the SBI column's next step is right, the rail for protection and credit is consent-based data, and that is where a distribution platform could matter.
Treat that as a question to chase, not a forecast.
